summary: A 1978 survey of ARPANET server hosts, testing how their FTP servers responded when mail was sent to an unknown recipient and when the MLFL command was used instead of MAIL. It reports results of two surveys run in late 1978.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 751 reports tests of ARPANET FTP servers. It records how servers responded to mail for an unknown recipient and whether they handled the MLFL command.

questions: how did early networks transfer mail
why did rfc 751 survey ftp servers
what did the rfc 751 ftp survey test
subtitle: A survey of how ARPANET FTP servers handled unknown recipients and the MLFL command.

tldr.problem: The survey sought to learn whether FTP servers accepted mail to unknown recipients and how widely they supported MLFL.
tldr.mechanism: The author tested mail commands at server hosts, recording replies to MAIL for an unlikely recipient and to MLFL for a known mailbox.
tldr.outcome: The report lists hosts and responses, documenting differing behavior across the servers tested.

today: RFC 751 is a survey report of ARPANET FTP server behavior during 1978. It documents the test methods and host responses rather than defining a required server behavior.

sections.title: What the Survey Tested
sections.content:
The RFC describes two surveys run between September 20 and December 11, 1978. One tested mail to an unknown recipient; the other tested MLFL instead of the usual MAIL command for a known recipient.

MLFL sends the message over a data connection rather than the command connection. The memo says this could avoid end-of-mail marker and command-reader problems.
sections.plainLanguage: The author tried two things at FTP servers: sending mail to a name unlikely to exist and sending mail with the MLFL command. The report records the replies.

sections.title: MLFL Responses
sections.content:
For the MLFL survey, the author connected to socket 3, sent MLFL, and followed server instructions for authentication or a data connection when requested. The report groups sites that failed or gave anomalous replies, sites that rejected the command as unrecognized, and sites that appeared to support it.

Some sites asked for USER NETML and PASS NETML before proceeding. The memo lists the tested hosts and the last reply or action for groups of results.
sections.plainLanguage: Some servers appeared to support MLFL, some reported that they did not recognize it, and some tests ended with an anomalous response or a connection problem.

sections.title: Mail to an Unknown Recipient
sections.content:
The MAIL survey sent the command “MAIL Fzorkness,” using a recipient the author considered unlikely to exist. The report lists sites that accepted the mail, refused it with different replies, did not support the command, or could not be reached.

The results are recorded as a survey, not as a protocol specification or a rule requiring all servers to behave alike.
sections.plainLanguage: The servers did not all answer the same way when asked to accept mail for Fzorkness. The tables show each reported response.
